name: Rajaportti Sauna
who: Wood-fired public bathhouse open since 1906, the oldest running public sauna in Finland, pay-per-visit with separate men's and women's sides.
why: Barely changed in over a century; the reference point for the working-class Finnish public-sauna tradition.

name: Kotiharjun Sauna
who: Helsinki's last wood-heated public courtyard sauna, running since 1928, open Tue-Sun afternoons, whisks and towels for rent.
why: The living link to Helsinki's vanished network of neighborhood saunas, still wood-fired and still open to anyone.

name: Loyly
who: Design-award-winning public sauna and restaurant on the Helsinki waterfront, timber-clad, walk-in and ticketed sessions, sea swimming off its own rocks.
why: The building that put contemporary Finnish sauna architecture on the world map and turned sauna-going into a destination outing.

name: Allas Sea Pool
who: Seaside lido in the harbor with three pools (seawater, warm, kids') plus sauna and cafe, open year-round with day tickets.
why: Central Helsinki's default sauna-and-swim social spot, floating right on the harbor water.

name: Kulttuurisauna
who: Minimalist wood-heated public sauna on the water in Merihaka, opened 2012 by architect Tuomas Toivonen and designer Nene Tsuboi, ticketed, caps group size to keep it quiet.
why: The architects' sauna: a small, deliberately calm counterpoint to Helsinki's bigger wellness venues, praised worldwide for its design.

name: Sompasauna
who: Free, volunteer-run wood-heated sauna village on the Helsinki shore, open 24/7, no staff, no booking, bring your own wood and towel.
why: The purest expression of Finnish sauna as commons: no owner, no fee, self-policed sauna peace, copied by grassroots groups across Europe.

name: Hellasgarden
who: Lakeside outdoor recreation area since the 1930s with wood-fired sauna huts, cold plunge, and a rowdy after-work sauna scene, day access and membership options.
why: Stockholm's oldest and most devoted sauna-and-lake club, where the after-work crowd has run its own rituals for decades.

name: KOK Oslo
who: Architect-designed floating saunas moored at Aker Brygge and Langkaia in the Oslo fjord, book-by-the-hour, wood-fired with fjord-water plunges.
why: The venue that turned floating sauna into an Oslo institution and a template copied around the Nordics.

name: Oslo Badstuforening
who: Non-profit sauna association running a fleet of named floating saunas (Maken, Stampen, Skarven, Havornen, Anda, Trosten) across the Oslo fjord, single tickets or membership, one fully wheelchair-accessible raft.
why: Built the fjord's floating-sauna network as a public-good project rather than a single luxury venue, scaling the format city-wide.

name: Therme Erding
who: The world's largest thermal spa complex, multiple sauna villages, Aufguss shows, water park, day tickets and multi-day passes.
why: Sheer scale defines it: no other thermal complex on earth packs in this much sauna, water, and staged Aufguss ritual under one roof.

name: vabali spa Berlin
who: Balinese-themed wellness resort with 13 saunas and steam baths, pools, a large sauna garden, and fireplace rooms, day-ticket access.
why: Berlin's biggest and most photographed sauna resort, credited with popularizing large-format Aufguss culture in the city.

name: Liquidrom
who: Domed urban spa in Kreuzberg built around a 36-degree saltwater pool with underwater sound and light, plus steam rooms and a Finnish sauna running Aufguss sessions, open daily.
why: A cult Berlin design object as much as a spa: light, sound, and water staged as one immersive room, unlike anything else in the segment.

name: Tropical Islands Resort
who: Sauna and spa complex inside a former airship hangar near Berlin, seven themed sauna areas modeled on Southeast Asian temple sites, professional Aufguss masters, day and overnight access.
why: Europe's largest tropical sauna complex, built at a scale and inside a structure no competitor can replicate.

name: Community Sauna Baths
who: Not-for-profit outdoor sauna and cold-plunge sites across Camberwell, Hackney Wick, Peckham, Stratford, and Walthamstow, book-by-the-slot barrel and cabin saunas.
why: The venue behind London's sauna boom, proving a cold-climate ritual could take root as a social habit in a city with no sauna tradition at all.

name: Sauna Deco
who: Boutique canal-house sauna and hammam built inside a 1920s Art Deco interior salvaged from the Paris department store Le Bon Marche, ticketed day sessions.
why: A one-off: no other sauna in the segment sits inside a protected Art Deco period interior in a city center canal house.

name: Iglupark
who: Igloo-shaped waterfront saunas and cabins at Noblessner Marina, bookable by the hour with guided sauna rituals.
why: Leads Tallinn's new wave of design-forward waterfront saunas, exporting the Baltic sauna revival to a marina setting.

name: Mooska Smoke Sauna Farm
who: Working farm in South Estonia offering guided sessions in a traditional Voromaa smoke sauna, the tradition UNESCO listed as Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2014, booking by appointment.
why: The clearest public gateway into a centuries-old smoke-sauna tradition that UNESCO itself recognizes as a living cultural practice, not a spa product.

name: SaunaLab Kanda
who: Design-led urban sauna facility in Kanda, Tokyo, women-friendly hours, midday-to-night booking, part of Japan's current sauna boom.
why: A flagship of Japan's design-driven sauna wave, built for the city's younger, gender-mixed sauna crowd rather than the old bathhouse model.
